unrecoverable.notes: Flo, scoping the zero-contrast rule (follow-up to cs2-batch 07d4cb): a mid-gradient APCA zero-crossing is not the same thing as exact-zero contrast between foreground and surface/background. The crossing is a single thin line orthogonal to the gradient; the role pairs are flat colors occupying large areas, so zero holds everywhere. Consequence: the hue-conditional tolerance for sign flips (birdsofprey) applies only to thin gradient crossings, never to flat role-pair contrast. A flat fg/surface pair at ~zero APCA is invalid regardless of hue separation.

- it clearly contains a very strong blue-to-white gradient
- it *only* contains blue and white
because of its limited "range" of hues, using a gradient as a background guarantees that both colors are used in the background (white and blue) and that the foreground colors (foreground and accent) will be almost impossible to distinguish in *at least some parts* of the gradient.

evidence.notes: This one is genuinely hard because the artwork is basically one big blue-to-white gradient, and so in that case we cannot really use a background to surface gradient to imitate it. Otherwise, there is for sure going to be some points in the gradient where the foreground cannot be distinguished from the background. So even though the artwork is very strongly a gradient, this is a rare case where we have to go flat. You can even see a case that should be forbidden, which is that the foreground and the background have the same color in option A's palette (or at least not visually distinguishable). This should give an APCA contrast of 0, which is strictly forbidden between foreground and background

evidence.label: gf-off
evidence.notes:
This artwork is an exception, because 
- it clearly contains a very strong blue-to-white gradient
- it *only* contains blue and white
because of its limited "range" of hues, using a gradient as a background guarantees that both colors are used in the background (white and blue) and that the foreground colors (foreground and accent) will be almost impossible to distinguish in *at least some parts* of the gradient.

There is technically a way to represent both: limit the background gradient to only a portion of the full range (for example deep blue Nazar to light blue Skinny Jeans) and then use the rest of the range for the foreground and accent. I did an example of this in "One palette you'd endorse" below.
